## Abstract {.unnumbered}

After the M7.5 earthquake that struck coastal Venezuela on 24 June 2026, at least eight
organisations released satellite-derived building-damage products. We evaluated the six that
published an analysed extent, scoring them not against a single expert reference but against
three with complementary blind spots: expert damage points from Copernicus EMS, crowd review of
AI-flagged locations, and 415 field reports. This lets the references check each other, and the
expert reference did not pass: it captured 94% of field-reported destroyed buildings but only
49% of those reported as significantly damaged. Every precision measured against it is
therefore a floor — Microsoft's rises from 0.08 to roughly 0.24 once crowd-confirmed damage is
counted.

At building level, every product performed poorly. As delivered, precision ranged from 0.01 to
0.08 (recall 0.31–0.69); even in the one damage-dense area where all six score best — the Caraballeda AOI, where
96% of the reference sits, it reached only 0.04–0.09. None separated itself from a null model
built on coastline distance, building density and shaking intensity, which matched or beat
three of the six there and four of the six across their full delivered footprints. At
neighbourhood scale the products are usable — they ranked sectors by damage burden reliably —
though the same null ranked those sectors about as well, so this is where the products work
rather than where they add.

The rest of their value lies in their disagreement. Requiring more products to agree traces a
usable operating curve, from flagging every building any product marked (97% of known damage,
but 26 visits per damaged building found) to flagging only unanimous buildings (93% of flags
correct, 18% of the damage). Counting agreement between methodologically independent products
roughly doubles the
accuracy of any single product and requires no weights, no training data and no reference,
which makes it the only method we tested that is both effective and computable during a
response; a learned fusion scores 18% higher but is fitted on the damage map responders are
still waiting for.

One product alone published per-building acquisition metadata, and it was the only one whose
principal failure could be diagnosed: flags that crowd reviewers judged 71% undamaged traced to
an area covered by a single satellite scene, processed with no cross-scene check. These
findings come from one event and should be read as a case study and a reusable evaluation
method, not as general laws.

## Introduction

In the first days after a major earthquake, responders need to know where the damage is
and how bad it is, before ground access is possible. Satellite-derived damage products
fill this window, and their supply has grown quickly. The 2026 Venezuela earthquake drew
products from a government rapid-mapping service (Copernicus EMS), academic radar groups
(Oregon State University; IMPACT Initiatives), optical AI pipelines (Microsoft AI for
Good; University of Houston; a WFP/LIST/CERN collaboration), debris modelling (UNEP/OCHA
Joint Environment Unit), and volunteer AI platforms (HOT fAIr, DISHA). These products
disagree with each other, sometimes dramatically. A coordinator receiving several of them
in the same week has no established way to decide which to trust, for what purpose, and
at what spatial scale.

Evaluations of such products usually score them against an expert-interpreted reference
and treat that reference as complete truth. The assumption deserves scrutiny. The
reference is produced under the same time pressure, from the same kinds of imagery, and
with the same physical limits as the products it judges. If the reference systematically
misses lighter damage, then every published precision figure is understated, and it is
understated most in exactly the damage class where products are weakest.

Our approach is to use three references instead of one, chosen so that their failure
modes do not overlap. An expert reference (CEMS) covers both error types but only inside
its mapped extents. A crowd reference (MapSwipe) saw only locations that AI products had
flagged, so it can refute false alarms but cannot see misses. A field reference (ChatMap)
contains only confirmed damage, so it can reveal misses but says nothing about false
alarms. Each reference is used only for the question it can answer, and the three can be
used to check each other.

The paper makes three contributions:

1. A corrected scorecard for the six evaluable products of this event, including
   estimates of how far below the truth the conventionally measured numbers sit, and the
   observation that per-building accuracy and area-ranking accuracy are almost unrelated.
2. An operational result: the number of products that agree on a building acts as a
   reliable operating point, and we price each setting in field visits per damaged
   building found, so that responders can choose a setting rather than being handed one.
3. A diagnostic result: with published per-building metadata and a crowd campaign, a
   product's main failure could be traced to its cause during the response itself. Five
   of the six products publish no such metadata, and their failures remain undiagnosable.

Everything here comes from one event in one coastal, dense-urban geography. The method
transfers; the specific numbers and rule orderings should be treated as hypotheses until
they are replicated. We identify a suitable replication event in the Discussion.

## The event and the products

An M7.5 earthquake, preceded about 40 seconds earlier by an M7.2, struck near Yumare on
the Venezuelan coast at 22:05 UTC on 24 June 2026. Severe damage was concentrated along
the La Guaira coastal strip, in western Caracas, and in several inland towns. Copernicus
EMS rapid mapping was activated the same night (EMSR884).

We evaluate the six products that published a defined or defensible analysed extent, that
is, the area the product actually examined (@tbl-products). Without an analysed extent,
neither misses nor false-alarm rates can be counted fairly, because "no flag" cannot be
distinguished from "never looked". Two further AI products (HOT fAIr and DISHA) published
no extent and are included in the availability inventory only. For analyses that combine
products, all products were mapped onto a common base of Overture building footprints. For
scoring against references, each product keeps its own native geometry. The reason for
this separation is explained in Methods.

| Product | Provider | Sensing basis | Analysed buildings | Damage flags* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft AI4G | Microsoft | very-high-res optical + AI classifier | 72,162 (own footprints) | 8,410 |
| IMPACT v2 | IMPACT Initiatives | Sentinel-1 radar coherence change | swath (~372 km²) | 22,954 |
| OSU | Oregon State Univ. / NASA | Sentinel-1 radar coherence change | swath (~471 km²) | 31,259 |
| UH QuakeDamage | Univ. of Houston | VHR optical (Vantor, author-confirmed) + vision model, graded footprints | 447,263 incl. intact | ~91k dmg/destroyed |
| LIST | WFP / LIST / CERN | ResNet on pre/post SAR imagery (provider-stated) | 163,225 | 15,904 in core region |
| UNEP debris | UNEP/OCHA JEU | SAR-derived debris mass per footprint | no extent (assumption, see Methods) | 96,046 |

: Products evaluated. *Flag counts as harmonised to the common footprint base within each
product's own region; totals differ from providers' native counts because of
footprint-base differences. OSU figures refer to its v0 delivery, the version available
during the response; a revised v1 arrived after the study window and is compared in
@sec-casestudy. {#tbl-products}

Radar and optical products fail in different ways, which matters later in the paper.
Optical products (Microsoft, UH) classify what damage looks like from above. Radar
coherence products (IMPACT, OSU) measure something else: whether the fine-scale
arrangement of radar reflectors inside each pixel stayed stable between satellite passes.
An intact building is a stable reflector and keeps high coherence; a collapse rearranges
the reflectors and coherence drops. Vegetation never holds coherence in the first place,
so coherence methods are largely immune to the farmland and vegetation changes that
produce false alarms in optical and amplitude-based methods. LIST also runs on radar —
a ResNet change-detection model over pre- and post-event SAR imagery, per the provider
(no methodology document accompanied the delivery) — but it is not a coherence measure,
so that immunity is not assumed for it; UNEP's debris mass is likewise SAR-derived. We
verify the coherence claim empirically below.

![Who analysed where. Each product's analysed extent, the five expert-mapped CEMS AOIs
(dashed black), and — in red, with the zoom frame below — the core region: the intersection of
the CEMS extents with all five extent-publishing products (~61 km²), where the head-to-head,
ensemble and fusion analyses live. The extents span three orders of magnitude, from
Microsoft's single coastal strip (210 km²) to LIST's two full Sentinel scenes (~224,000
km²) — the reason the as-delivered and best-case frames of @sec-crossexam differ so much.
UH publishes no extent; its polygon is derived from its own classified footprints
(ADR-0018). UNEP publishes none at all and is scored under the stated coverage
assumption.](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/fig_extents_map.png){#fig-extents}

## Three references, three failure modes {#sec-refs}

![The three reference datasets at a glance. Two of them are HOT-run and easily confused:
**MapSwipe** is remote volunteers voting on ~50 m hex cells (not building points), used to
adjudicate false alarms; **ChatMap** is field teams reporting building-level points from the
ground, used to reveal misses. They are used separately, each only for the error type its
geometry and sampling permit.](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/reference_architecture.png){#fig-refarch}

**Copernicus EMS (CEMS) building-damage points.** Trained analysts interpret
very-high-resolution imagery and mark each damaged building as a graded point. Within its
mapped extents we treat this as reference grade for both error types, under one explicit
assumption: a building without a CEMS point, inside an area CEMS analysed, is genuinely
undamaged. We use the latest monitoring product for each area (3,119 points, of which
1,467 damaged-or-destroyed points fall inside the core comparison region). The rest of
the paper tests the completeness assumption directly (@sec-crossexam).

**MapSwipe crowd validation.** A Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team campaign in which more
than 400 volunteers reviewed roughly 8,000 locations where an AI product had flagged
damage, voting "damaged", "no damage", or "not sure" on each ~50 m cell. The median cell
received 6–13 votes; we require at least 4 votes and take the majority. Four is a quorum
rather than a tuned threshold: every completed project delivered at least four votes on
every cell, so the rule's effect is to exclude cells from the unfinished follow-up
projects, which averaged about one vote per cell, where a verdict would rest on a single
volunteer. Volunteers only ever saw AI-flagged places, so this dataset can adjudicate
false alarms but can never reveal a missed building.

**ChatMap field reports.** 415 damage points reported from the ground by field teams and
graded minimal, significant, or complete. A ground observation is strong evidence that
damage is real, but the collection was opportunistic, with no defined survey area, so the
absence of a point means nothing. This dataset measures misses and cannot measure false
alarms. Its points extend inland well beyond the CEMS extents.

Used together, the three references cover each other's blind spots. CEMS provides the
two-sided scorecard inside its bounds. ChatMap measures what CEMS and the products miss.
MapSwipe settles disputes between a product and CEMS on the false-alarm side.

**Which reference is used where.** CEMS is the primary reference: every headline precision
and recall in this paper is computed against it, at r = 10 m, unless labelled otherwise.
The other two enter only for the questions their geometry permits. ChatMap plays two
distinct roles from the same 415 points: *unioned* with CEMS it forms a fuller
building-level reference (both are damage points), and *held separate* it is what exposes
CEMS's own grade-blindness (@sec-crossexam) — the same dataset, two purposes, never
conflated. MapSwipe is a lens rather than a reference: its verdicts are per ~50 m cell and
were collected only over AI-flagged locations, so it can adjudicate false alarms (the
crowd-adjusted precision) and probe CEMS's completeness, but it cannot serve as a
building-level reference or fairly score a model it never saw — for instance the geography
baseline of @sec-dial, which it would penalise for flags the crowd never adjudicated. We
keep CEMS-only as the default because unioning ChatMap changes nothing material: across all
six products it lifts precision by at most 0.006 and recall by at most 0.026. Where the
strengthened value carries signal we report it in parentheses, e.g. Microsoft precision
0.081 (0.087).

## Methods

### Matching products to references

The product and reference use different geometries — CEMS drops points on damaged
buildings, while each product flags its own footprints on its own building base — so there
is no shared list of instances on which to build a single confusion matrix. We therefore
score by *proximity*, the standard approach for detection-style evaluation: precision
anchors on the product (of its flagged buildings, how many have a CEMS damage point within
radius r?), and recall anchors on the reference (of the CEMS damage points, how many have a
product flag within r?). Each metric carries its own denominator. Because the two metrics
are precision and recall, neither uses the undamaged background (true negatives) — which we
could not enumerate anyway, since CEMS never labels the undamaged stock.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Dual-anchored matching. Left: a product is scored only where it AND the reference both looked. Middle: recall anchors on the reference — each CEMS damage point asks whether a product flag lies within radius r. Right: precision anchors on the product — each flagged building asks whether a CEMS point lies within r. Each metric brings its own denominator."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mp
import numpy as np
from shapely.geometry import Point

R = 0.16
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 5.1))
a0 = ax[0]
c1, c2 = Point(-0.28, 0).buffer(0.75), Point(0.28, 0).buffer(0.75)
inter = c1.intersection(c2)
a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(inter.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="#c8e6c9", ec="none"))
for c, col, lab, xy in ((c1, "tab:blue", "CEMS analysed extent", (-0.75, 0.62)),
                        (c2, "tab:orange", "product AOI", (0.42, 0.62))):
    a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(c.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="none", ec=col, lw=2))
    a0.annotate(lab, xy, fontsize=9, color=col)
a0.annotate("scored HERE only", (0, -0.05), fontsize=10, ha="center", weight="bold", color="#2e7d32")
a0.set_title("1 · where scoring happens", fontsize=10)
a1 = ax[1]
for x, y in [(-0.38, 0.22), (0.05, -0.32), (-0.6, -0.5), (0.62, -0.15)]:
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.3, True), (0.15, -0.25, True), (0.45, 0.42, False)]:
    a1.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
    a1.annotate("TP" if hit else "FN (missed)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=9,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a1.set_title("2 · RECALL — anchor on each CEMS point", fontsize=10)
a2 = ax[2]
for x, y in [(-0.36, 0.25), (0.2, -0.14)]:
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.32, True), (0.1, -0.2, True), (0.5, 0.45, False), (-0.15, -0.6, False)]:
    a2.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
    a2.annotate("TP" if hit else "FP (false alarm)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=9,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a2.set_title("3 · PRECISION — anchor on each product flag", fontsize=10)
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlim(-1.05, 1.05); a.set_ylim(-1.0, 0.9)
    a.set_aspect("equal"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
h = [plt.Line2D([], [], marker="*", ls="", ms=13, c="k", label="CEMS damage point"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], marker="s", ls="", ms=8, c="tab:orange", label="product-flagged building"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], ls="--", c="grey", label="match radius r")]
fig.legend(handles=h, loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 0.97))
plt.show()
```

A product is only accountable where both it and the reference actually looked, so all
scoring is restricted to the intersection of analysed extents; @fig-extents maps every
extent this paper scores against, and the core region they share. UNEP debris publishes no
extent. Based on its density across the study region, we make the explicit assumption
that it fully covers the ~61 km² core comparison region, the same logic used for its
stand-alone evaluation in fully enclosed administrative units.

An analysed extent says where a product looked, not whether it could see. Cloud can hide
individual buildings inside a declared extent. Only Microsoft publishes a per-building
visibility field, and a robustness check against it found the effect negligible in this
event: 3.6% of buildings are mostly obscured, precision is unchanged under any visibility
filter, and exactly one missed reference point falls on an obscured building. The model
abstains under cloud rather than flagging into it. We therefore score all products
without visibility corrections, noting that the check is impossible for the five products
that publish no such field.

The matching radius comes from the urban fabric rather than from convenience. The median
distance between neighbouring building centroids in the core region is 9.7 m, and 93% of
buildings have a neighbour within 20 m. We therefore use r = 10 m as the largest radius
at which "did the product flag this building" is still a meaningful question. Larger
radii answer a different and equally legitimate question, namely whether the flag put a
responder within sight of real damage. We use named scales for those: 30 m (line of
sight), 60 m (same block), 100 m (right area).

**The measurement frames used in this paper.** Because the analyses ask different
questions, they use different matching frames, and numbers are not comparable across
frames. To keep them straight:

| frame | radius | matched against | used for | why this radius |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary** *(default everywhere)* | **10 m** | CEMS points | all precision/recall, the pairwise rules, the voting table, the learned fusion and the geography null | tight enough that a flag must land on or beside the right building |
| **Line-of-sight** | **30 m** | CEMS points | coverage and visits-per-find columns of @tbl-dial only | answers a different question: "would a responder sent here *see* the damage" |
| **Field** | **20 m** | ChatMap field points | recall against ground reports only | absorbs phone-GPS error in the field reports |

: The measurement frames. Every CEMS-based number in this paper uses the 10 m primary frame,
so all of them are directly comparable. The two exceptions exist because they answer different
questions or use a different reference, and are always labelled where used.
{#tbl-allframes}

Earlier drafts of this work reported the fusion analysis at a 20 m radius while the headline
figures used 10 m, which made two sets of precision values circulate that were not comparable.
That is resolved: **everything CEMS-based is now reported at 10 m**. The 20 m radius survives in
one place only, as a sensitivity frame. The concern that kept it was fit stability — a
per-building model needs enough positives in each spatial block, and halving the radius halves
the positive class (2,733 buildings labelled damaged at 20 m, 1,350 at 10 m). Each frame is
therefore self-contained: every model is fitted *and* evaluated at a single radius, the
reported numbers come from the 10 m fit, and the full 20 m refit is in the Appendix
(@tbl-radius). The two fits support the same conclusions — no single product separates from
the null, combination does — which is the evidence the tighter label did not starve the fit.

These are not four different measurement philosophies, and it is worth being precise about
what actually separates them, because the wrong picture makes the numbers look arbitrary.
Matching a flag to a reference point by building centroid rather than by native geometry turns
out to be worth almost nothing: re-running the fusion analysis at r = 10 m reproduces the
scorecard precisions to within 0.005 for every product (Microsoft 0.081 against 0.080, OSU
0.045 against 0.040, and so on). **The only thing that materially separates these frames is the
radius.** Microsoft's precision is 0.08 at 10 m and 0.138 at 20 m; the same product, the same
flags, the same reference, and two different definitions of what counts as a hit.

That leaves the one frame not yet described:

- **Fusion frame** (building-centroid matching against CEMS, r = 10 m like everything else):
  used in the learned-fusion section, where every building needs a label rather than only the
  flagged ones. Its 20 m refit — every precision 1.6–2.2× higher, the same conclusions — is
  the Appendix sensitivity frame (@tbl-radius); only within-frame comparisons are valid.

Before the numbers, one point about what the radius *is*, because it is easy to picture it as a
tolerance applied to the products alone. It is not. The radius defines the **label** — the
target every predictor is trained and scored against:

> A building counts as damaged if a CEMS damage point lies within *r* metres of it.

Nothing else in the analysis carries a radius. The geography null's inputs are coast distance,
building density and shaking intensity; none of them knows anything about *r*. What changes when
*r* changes is the definition of the truth all predictors are chasing. In the core region, r =
20 m labels about 2,733 buildings damaged and r = 10 m about 1,350 — half as many positives
from the identical CEMS points. This matters for interpretation: a wide radius smears each
reference point into a small blob of neighbouring buildings, making the target patchy and
area-shaped, which is precisely the shape a smooth geography surface predicts well. A tighter
radius concentrates the positives onto individual buildings, where per-building discrimination
is required. The comparison between products and the null is therefore mildly radius-dependent,
and we quantify that below rather than leave it implicit.

One reassurance follows from holding the radius fixed. The learned-fusion analysis matches
flags to reference points by building centroid, while the headline scorecard matches on native
geometry, and it would be reasonable to worry that this alone shifts the numbers. It does not.
Evaluated at the same 10 m radius, the two agree to within 0.005 for every product:

| product | scorecard (native geometry) | fusion analysis (centroid) | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| UH | 0.090 | 0.093 | +0.003 |
| UNEP | 0.090 | 0.086 | −0.004 |
| Microsoft | 0.080 | 0.081 | +0.001 |
| IMPACT | 0.070 | 0.069 | −0.001 |
| LIST | 0.060 | 0.057 | −0.003 |
| OSU | 0.040 | 0.045 | +0.005 |

: Precision at r = 10 m under the two matching methods. Centroid versus native-geometry
matching is worth at most 0.005; once the radius is held fixed the two are effectively the same
measurement. {#tbl-frames}

This is why the earlier inconsistency mattered so much and is worth stating plainly: the large
gaps between numbers in earlier drafts were caused *entirely* by the radius, not by any
difference in matching method or philosophy. With the radius now fixed at 10 m throughout,
every CEMS-based precision in this paper is directly comparable to every other.

### Area ranking and error structure

For questions about where damage is concentrated, we aggregate per-building flags to
hexagonal grid cells at two sizes, roughly 0.74 km² and 5.2 km² (the larger approximates
a triage sector), and compare each product's ranking of cells against the ranking implied
by CEMS, using rank correlation and top-k overlap.

Whether a ranking survives noisy per-building labels depends on how the noise is arranged
in space, so we test that directly. A Poisson regression predicts each cell's flag count
from its CEMS damage count, with the cell's building stock as an exposure offset so that
"more flags because more buildings" cannot register as bias. The residuals, meaning over-
or under-flagging not explained by real damage, are then tested in two ways: for spatial
clustering, using Moran's I with significance from permutations over the same cell
lattice (this controls for the shape of the built-up area itself), and for correlation
with variables that would corrupt a ranking, namely building density, distance to the
coast, and modelled shaking intensity.

### Combining products, and adjudicating disagreements with the reference

For per-building questions, each product's flags are projected onto the shared Overture
footprint base and combined by voting. A building passes the "k-of-6" rule when at least
k of the six products flag it. Throughout the paper, k-of-6 names a rule, never a score.
Voting rules are scored exactly as single products are.

Because CEMS itself has gaps, precision measured against CEMS is a lower bound. A
reference gap can turn a correct flag into an apparent false positive, but never the
reverse, so the true precision lies at or above the measured value. We estimate how far
above by adjudication: for every flagged building with no CEMS point within 10 m, we look
up the MapSwipe majority verdict for its cell and count the share that volunteers judged
damaged. "Crowd-adjusted precision" adds those confirmed flags back to the numerator.
Each precision estimate in this paper is therefore an interval, from the CEMS-measured
lower bound to the crowd-adjusted value. One caveat sets the character of the upper end:
MapSwipe verdicts are per ~50 m cell, not per building (@fig-refarch), so a
crowd-confirmed flag means "damage somewhere in this cell," not "this building." The
crowd-adjusted value is therefore an *upper* estimate of building-level precision, and the
truth lies between it and the CEMS floor. How stable is that crowd verdict? In
July–August 2026, after this paper's data freeze, an independent second crowd re-voted the
identical Catia La Mar cells with nearly three times as many votes per cell. Any single
cell's verdict proved noisy — with about six votes, much of what separates one cell's
verdict from another's is voting luck — but the number the adjustment is actually built
on, the share of a product's unmatched flags the crowd confirms, barely moved: 13.2%
under the first crowd, 11.5% under the second. The upper estimates in this paper should
therefore be read as sitting slightly high; the mechanism and the full re-test are shown
in the Appendix (@fig-crowdmech). A second, independent check uses ChatMap instead:
because its field points are building-level, they can be unioned directly with the CEMS
points, which raises measured precision by a smaller, sharper 5–9% (the field data is
sparse — 415 points — but geometrically exact).

Recall has no such correction, and its bias runs the other way. Adjudication re-judges
flags; it cannot add the damage CEMS never recorded to recall's denominator — the crowd
saw only AI-flagged places, and the field reports are positives-only with no survey
frame, so the full denominator is unknowable. Because the reference over-represents
destruction, which is the damage class every product detects best, recall measured
against it is flattered rather than understated. The rule of thumb for this whole paper:
**against an incomplete reference, measured precision is a floor and measured recall is
a ceiling.** The grade-stratified field-frame measurements in @sec-crossexam quantify
how much the recall ceiling gives back.

### The geography null model and weighted fusion {#sec-dayzero}

Two of this paper's constructions are models rather than products, and both are built the
same way. The **geography null model** exists to calibrate what the accuracy numbers mean: it
asks how much of the damage pattern is recoverable from coarse spatial structure and shaking
alone, so that a product's score can be read against something other than zero. It uses three
context variables computed per building, all available within hours of the shaking: distance
to the coastline (metres), local building density (buildings per H3 res-9 cell, ~0.1 km²), and
ground-motion intensity from the USGS ShakeMap (MMI). These predict per-building CEMS damage
(grades {2,3}) through a class-balanced logistic regression. Validation is **spatially
blocked**: the model is trained and scored on disjoint ~5 km² zones, because neighbouring
buildings share both their features and their labels, and a random train/test split would leak
that structure into an inflated score (@fig-dayzero-build).

Because a null is only meaningful if it is the *strongest* honest account of "just geography" —
a weak one would flatter the products by construction — we fit every feature set with both a
class-balanced logistic regression and a random forest (400 trees, minimum leaf 20), and report
whichever scores higher in that frame, disclosing both:

| feature set | random forest | logistic |
|---|---|---|
| all inputs (weighted fusion) | 0.283 | 0.284 |
| context only, core region | 0.045 | **0.060** |
| context only, full delivered footprints | **stronger for 5 of 6** | stronger for MS only |
| products only | 0.258 | 0.271 |

: Average precision by learner and feature set, spatial-block CV. Where products are involved
the learner is irrelevant; for the null it is not, and which learner wins depends on the
frame. {#tbl-learners}

Wherever products enter, the two learners are indistinguishable, so no fusion result depends on
that choice. The null is a different matter, and the two analysis layers do not agree on which
model represents geography better. In the compact core region the logistic wins (0.060 against
0.045): shaking is near-constant there and the remaining relationship is smooth, so the forest
mostly fits block-specific structure that does not generalise. Across the full delivered
footprints the ranking reverses for five of six products, sometimes sharply, because those regions span real variation in shaking that
interacts non-linearly with coast distance and density. We therefore use the logistic null in
the core-region analysis and the forest null in the as-delivered analysis, which is simply the
rule stated above applied twice. That the two layers need different model classes to describe
geography well is itself a signal that they are different regimes — the same conclusion the
feature importances reach below.

We call it a *null model* rather than a baseline, and deliberately avoid naming it after
day zero, because the distinction is easy to blur and consequential. Its three inputs are genuinely
available on day zero; its fitted coefficients are not. Estimating them requires the very
damage labels a responder is waiting for, so the model cannot be run on the day it names. It
is not an alternative anyone could have deployed. What it provides instead is a reference
level — the standard role of a null model, like a majority-class or stratified-random
comparator — and because we allow it to be fitted with hindsight, it is a *generous* null. The
two directions therefore read differently. A product that beats it has demonstrated real
information beyond spatial structure, and the inference is strong precisely because the null
was given every advantage. A product that loses to it has flags placed no better than an
obvious retrospective geography prior, which is a serious finding about that product — but it
is not a claim that geography was an available substitute.

How much the null knows about *this* earthquake also depends on which of the paper's two
analysis layers it is fitted in, and the difference is stark. Within the Caraballeda core
region, ShakeMap intensity is effectively constant, and its measured importance is exactly
0.000: there, the model runs on distance-to-coast and density alone, both static, and carries
no event-specific information whatsoever. Its skill in that layer is a hindsight description
of where damage happened to fall. Across the full delivered footprints, which span far more
ground and much more variation in shaking, MMI carries 0.25–0.31 of the importance, and the
null is genuinely using event information. The exception proves the mechanism: Microsoft
shipped only the coastal strip, so its footprint nearly coincides with the core region and its
MMI importance falls back to 0.000. The as-delivered comparison is consequently the better
founded of the two, and the core-region comparison should be read strictly as a null.

Two aspects of the fitting deserve to be separated, because they carry different risks. The
model's *coefficients* are estimated strictly out-of-fold: each building's score comes from a
forest that never saw its block, so no building is graded by a model trained on it. The
*decision threshold* — the cut that turns the continuous risk into a flag list — is a second,
separate choice, and where a single operating point is reported we select it inside the
training folds and apply it blind to the held-out data, so that it too is never fitted to the
scores it is judged on. Only the first of these is handled by cross-validation; the second is
a separate operation that blocked CV does nothing to protect. The difference it makes here is
small: selecting the cut out-of-sample yields F1 0.129 against 0.128 for a cut chosen in
hindsight (@sec-dial) — a difference of 0.001, i.e. none. That is a fact about
this sample size — a single scalar estimated from hundreds of thousands of buildings is pinned
down closely either way — and not a general licence: on a small reference the same shortcut
could flatter a model materially, and the distinction is worth preserving in the method.

The model's output is a continuous per-building risk in [0, 1], not a flag list — and that
distinction governs how it is compared. Any threshold on the score defines a flag list, so
sweeping the threshold traces a whole *family* of no-satellite predictors: a full
precision–recall curve. A single product, by contrast, is one binary flag list — one point
in that plane, because the provider already fixed the threshold. The two are therefore
compared point-against-curve, or summarised by average precision (the area under the PR
curve), a quantity that is defined for a continuous score but degenerate for a binary one.
It is worth being exact about the degeneracy, because the intuition that a one-point
predictor's AP simply *is* its precision is close but wrong, and the difference is what
misleads. Average precision is a recall-weighted sum over the steps of the PR curve, and a
binary flag list has two: the flagged set itself, and the trivial "flag everything" endpoint.
It therefore evaluates to
$$\mathrm{AP}_{\text{binary}} = P\cdot R + (1-R)\cdot \pi$$
where $\pi$ is the prevalence of damage. The second term is free credit that any predictor
whatsoever collects for the flag-everything endpoint. Because $\pi$ (0.023 here) is far below
every product's precision, that term drags each product's AP *down toward prevalence*, and it
does so hardest for the products with the lowest recall. The effect is to compress genuinely
different products into a narrow band — 0.042–0.055 across our six, whose precisions actually
range from 0.045 to 0.093 — sitting right where a mediocre continuous score also lands (the
forest null's AP is 0.045).
Two products can share an AP because one has high precision and low recall while the other
has the reverse; the number conceals exactly the trade-off an operational reader cares about.
This is why we report AP only among
the continuous scores — the geography null, flat voting, and weighted fusion — and place the products
as points, never as AP bars beside them. The **weighted fusion** adds the six product flags
and their confidence fields to these same three context variables, so the geography null is
that model with the product inputs ablated away. One detail matters for reading the numbers
literally: the headline fusion is reported from a logistic regression, which here scores
identically to a random forest (AP 0.28 either way), while the ablations — the null and its
products-only mirror — are both fitted with the forest, so that the two ablations are directly
comparable to each other. Both are refit for each frame they are reported in — on the small core region for the
fusion result (@sec-dial) and on each product's full delivered footprint for the
as-delivered benchmark (@sec-crossexam) — always under the same blocked validation. Two
cautions: the learned weights are calibrated to this single event and should not be assumed
to transfer, and within the small core region the ShakeMap term is nearly constant, so the
null-model skill there comes mostly from coast distance and density.

Two questions of fairness follow from putting a fitted model beside an unfitted product, and
both deserve explicit answers. The first is whether the two are scored on the same data. They
are. Cross-validation here is not a subsample of the evaluation: the folds partition the
buildings, every building sits in exactly one held-out fold, and its score is the prediction
of a model that never saw it. So the model and the products are scored on **identical
building sets with identical denominators** — the resampling only guarantees that no model is
graded on data it was trained on, which makes the models' numbers *more* conservative, not
less. The second question is the one that genuinely bites, and it runs in the models' favour:
the geography null model is fitted to *this event's* reference labels. Spatial blocking stops it
from memorising a building's neighbours, but each fold still learns event-level structure —
how steeply damage falls off with distance from this coastline, at this shaking level. A
responder on the actual day zero possessed no such fitted coefficient. The geography null model
should therefore be read as an **upper bound on geography-only skill for this event**: the
best a three-variable context model could have done *had it known* the event's damage
gradient. The products, by contrast, never saw the reference at all. The defensible claim is
consequently one about information content — *the six products add little building-level
information beyond what three context variables already carry* — and not the operational
claim that responders held this null model in hand on day zero. We return to this in the
Limitations.

![How the geography null model is built. Three context variables known within hours of the
earthquake — coast distance, building density, and ShakeMap intensity — feed one
spatially-blocked model whose target is CEMS damage; a class-balanced logistic regression and a
random forest are both fitted, and whichever scores higher in a given frame is the one reported
(the logistic in this core region, the forest across the larger delivered footprints of
@sec-crossexam). Its output is a *continuous*
per-building risk, so every threshold on it is a different flag list and the score traces an
entire precision–recall curve, against which a single product is one already-thresholded
point. No satellite product enters this model. Note what the diagram cannot show: fitting it
requires the damage labels themselves, which is why it is a retrospective null rather than
something available on the day its inputs
are.](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8_dayzero_schematic.png){#fig-dayzero-build}

## Results I — building-level accuracy is poor, area ranking is not {#sec-scorecard}

Scored per building at r = 10 m against CEMS, every product performed poorly — and how
poorly depends on a choice of frame that this paper refuses to make silently. Scored *as
delivered* — each product across everything CEMS mapped, which is what a responder
actually received — precision ranged from 0.009 to 0.081. Restricted to the
damage-dense Caraballeda AOI, where the products score best and 96% of the reference
lives (@sec-crossexam), precision ranged from 0.04 to 0.09 and recall from 0.31 to
0.69. Even in that best case, for every flag that matched a CEMS damage point, ten to
twenty did not. The rest of this paper quotes the best-case numbers unless labeled
otherwise, because outside Caraballeda the reference is too thin to interpret failure
cleanly — but the as-delivered figures are the operationally honest ones, since no
responder knew in advance which zones the products would get right.

A baseline puts them in perspective. Three variables are available within hours of any
earthquake, before a single satellite is tasked: distance to the coast, neighbourhood
building density, and the USGS ShakeMap intensity estimate. A model given only these
context variables, and no satellite observations at all, performs comparably to the products
themselves at building level (the comparison is made formally in @sec-dial, in that section's
own measurement frame: F1 0.128 for geography against 0.148 for the best product and
0.085–0.142 for the rest, with three of the six falling below it even at their own list
sizes). One caveat governs the reading throughout: this model is fitted to the event's own
damage labels, so it is a retrospective diagnostic rather than something a responder could
have run — the claim is about how much information the products add over coarse spatial
structure, not about what was operationally in hand. Under that reading, no individual product
demonstrated building-level skill clearly beyond what coastline distance, building density and
shaking already encode — while their *combination* did, which is the more useful finding.

The area-level picture is different in kind, though not in the way that flatters the products.
At the ~5 km² sector scale, Microsoft and OSU correctly identified 80–85% of the 20 worst-hit
cells (rank correlation ρ ≈ 0.57), and ranking skill improved as cells got coarser, because the
per-building noise averages out. This is the scale at which the products are genuinely usable.
It is not, however, a scale at which they demonstrate information beyond geography: the same
null model ranks these cells better for five of the six products (@tbl-nullrank) — though that
comparison is dominated by telling Caraballeda apart from the quiet AOIs; within Caraballeda the
six split evenly against it.
Area ranking is therefore where these products *work*, not where they *add* — a distinction we
return to in the Discussion.

Because area ranking is the products' strongest result, it deserves the same null test as the
building-level numbers. We aggregated the geography null's out-of-fold predicted probabilities
to exactly the cells used above — its expected damage count per cell, needing no threshold —
and correlated those with the CEMS count the same way:

| scale | product | ρ product | ρ geography null | difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ~5 km² (res 7) | Microsoft | 0.585 | **0.631** | -0.046 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | OSU | **0.540** | 0.485 | +0.055 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | IMPACT v2 | 0.433 | **0.673** | -0.240 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | LIST | 0.404 | **0.500** | -0.096 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | UNEP | 0.220 | **0.501** | -0.281 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | UH | -0.085 | **0.701** | -0.786 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | OSU | **0.505** | 0.478 | +0.027 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | Microsoft | 0.466 | **0.568** | -0.102 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | IMPACT v2 | 0.292 | **0.594** | -0.303 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | LIST | 0.276 | **0.445** | -0.169 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | UNEP | 0.068 | **0.451** | -0.383 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | UH | -0.114 | **0.580** | -0.694 |

: Spearman rank correlation with the CEMS damage count per cell, product against
geography null, on identical cells within each product's shared region, all six
evaluated products. Only OSU exceeds the null, at either scale. {#tbl-nullrank}

The result is uncomfortable but clear: **geography alone ranks these areas better than the
products do**, beating five of the six at the sector scale and five of six again at the finer
scale. The margins are not marginal — IMPACT 0.673 against 0.433, UNEP 0.501 against 0.220 —
and UH's rank correlation is *negative* (−0.085), meaning its sector ordering is slightly worse
than no information at all. Only OSU is ahead of the null, and only narrowly (0.540 against
0.485).

That comparison spans all five mapped areas, however, and 96% of the reference damage sits in
one of them. Much of what it rewards is therefore the coarse discrimination of Caraballeda from
four quiet AOIs — a task coastline distance and building density solve almost by definition. The
sharper question is whether the products can out-rank geography *within* the damage zone, and
there the picture is different. Restricting every region to Caraballeda and re-running at
~0.7 km² cells, the six split evenly: LIST (0.668 against 0.543), OSU (0.642 against 0.562) and
IMPACT (0.548 against 0.456) beat the null, while Microsoft (0.466 against 0.568), UNEP (0.451
against 0.524) and UH (0.389 against 0.597) fall below it; at ~0.1 km² the same three-three
split holds. **So the products do carry real information about where within a damaged area to
go first — what they do not add is knowledge of which area that is**, which is the part
geography already encodes. The headline five-of-six should be read as a statement about the
coarse task, not as evidence that the products are uninformative at every scale.

| product | ρ product | ρ geography null | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| LIST | 0.668 | 0.543 | +0.125 |
| IMPACT v2 | 0.548 | 0.456 | +0.092 |
| OSU | 0.642 | 0.562 | +0.080 |
| UNEP | 0.451 | 0.524 | -0.074 |
| Microsoft | 0.466 | 0.568 | -0.102 |
| UH | 0.389 | 0.597 | -0.208 |

: The same test restricted to the Caraballeda AOI, ~0.7 km² cells. Within the damage
zone the six split evenly against the null, and the same three-three split holds at
~0.1 km². {#tbl-nullrank-cara}

The interpretation is otherwise the same as at building level, and
carries the same limitation. The null is fitted on this event's damage labels, so this says the
damage pattern was largely recoverable from coastline distance, building density and shaking
*in hindsight* — not that a responder had this ranking available on day one, which they did not
and the products were. What it does rule out is the reading that area ranking demonstrates the
products are extracting damage information the geography does not already contain. At this
scale they are reproducing a spatial pattern, competently, that was largely predictable from
the map.

The error-structure test explains why ranking survives. The residual over-flagging is
strongly clustered in space (Moran's I 0.45–0.60, p = 0.001 for each of the three
products this test covers — Microsoft, IMPACT, and OSU, the members whose extents
overlap CEMS broadly enough for the cell-level regression; extending it to the newer
members is open work), so the errors are not random noise. But once building stock is controlled, the clustering
follows the earthquake itself: residuals rise toward the coast and with modelled shaking,
and show no association with building density. A direct test of the concern that flags
merely reproduce the building map is also negative once exposure is controlled. In short,
the products over-call most where damage is genuinely worst. That error structure
preserves area rankings. The dangerous alternative, errors that track urban form, is what
the test rules out.

![Exposure-adjusted residual maps (red = over-flagging beyond what CEMS damage
explains) for the three products the error-structure test covers. Each panel autoscales
to its own analysed region, which is why they look so different: Microsoft analysed a
single ~30 km coastal strip, so its few hundred grid cells appear as individual dots,
while IMPACT and OSU are Sentinel-1 swaths spanning roughly 200 km, whose thousands of
cells merge visually. IMPACT and OSU residuals follow the coastal severity gradient.
Microsoft's error is a single hard cluster at the west end of its
region.](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3_residual_maps_res8.png)

One product does not fit this benign pattern. Microsoft's residual error is not a
gradient but a single dense cluster in the western coastal strip, and no covariate
explains it. At this point in the analysis we cannot say what the cluster is: real
over-detection and a local gap in the reference would look identical. Section
@sec-casestudy resolves the question with the other two references.

That ambiguity applies to every number in this section, not just the anomaly. Everything
above assumes CEMS is complete within its extents. The next section tests that
assumption.

## Results II — testing the reference itself {#sec-crossexam}

**CEMS misses about half of significant damage.** We scored CEMS itself against the 415
field-reported damage points that fall inside its extents, using r = 20 m to absorb
phone-GPS error (@tbl-field). The result is a consistent gradient by damage grade.

| dataset scored | "complete" damage found | "significant" found | "minimal" found |
|---|---|---|---|
| CEMS (expert reference) | **0.94** | **0.49** | 0.17 |
| OSU | 0.92 | 0.71 | 0.21 |
| LIST | 0.83 | 0.70 | 0.21 |
| Microsoft | 0.82 | 0.33 | — |
| IMPACT v2 | 0.73 | 0.46 | 0.25 |
| UNEP debris (core region) | 0.66 | 0.23 | — |
| UH | 0.59 | 0.23 | 0.45 |
| any of the six products (union, core region) | 0.97 | 0.87 | — |

: How much ground-truthed damage each dataset caught, by damage grade. Every row —
including CEMS — is scored against the ChatMap field points, the one reference that can
measure the expert reference's own misses. Each cell is the share of field-reported
damage points of that grade that the dataset flagged within 20 m; each dataset is scored
only on the points inside its own analysed extent (UNEP, which publishes none, is scored
in the core comparison region under the coverage assumption stated in Methods), so
denominators differ by row (complete: 316–328 points; significant: 47–63; minimal:
11–24, with cells left blank below 10 points). The union row combines the six products
and does not include CEMS. Minimal-grade cells are indicative only; confidence intervals
are pending. {#tbl-field}

Every satellite product, and the expert reference itself, detects destruction well and
lighter damage poorly. CEMS matched 94% of field-reported complete destruction but only
49% of significant damage within its own mapped extents. The same asymmetry has been
reported independently for the platform behind the Microsoft product, evaluated on the
2023 Turkey earthquakes (Ramachandran et al. 2025): 43% sensitivity — the same quantity
we call recall — against 94% specificity, the share of *intact* buildings correctly left
unflagged. High specificity with low sensitivity is precisely the signature of a detector
that only sees destruction, so this appears to be a general property of imagery-based
damage assessment rather than a quirk of this event.

Three consequences follow. First, satellite damage detection is, in practice,
destruction detection. Totals derived from it undercount the damaged-but-standing
buildings that dominate shelter needs. Second, every precision figure in @sec-scorecard
is a lower bound, and the bias is largest exactly where damage is lighter. Third, the
mirror image for recall: CEMS's damage list over-represents destruction, the class
products find best, so recall measured against CEMS is flattered — a ceiling, where
precision has a floor. @fig-gradeslope shows the corrective measurement: when the
denominator is field-reported *significant* damage instead of destruction, recall drops
for every dataset (CEMS 0.94 → 0.49; the six-product union 0.97 → 0.87; Microsoft
0.82 → 0.33).

![Recall by damage grade, field frame. Each line is one dataset's recall against
field-reported damage, at "complete" destruction versus "significant" damage. Every line
slopes down — the products and the expert reference alike find lighter damage far less
often. Because CEMS's own damage list is destruction-heavy, any recall measured against
it inherits the left end of these slopes: measured recall is a ceiling on true recall,
just as measured precision is a floor on true
precision.](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2e_grade_slope.png){#fig-gradeslope}

**Crowd review shows the lower bounds sit well below the truth.** For each product we
took the flags with no CEMS match and looked up the crowd's verdict on them. Counting the
crowd-confirmed flags as correct raises Microsoft's per-building precision from 0.08 to
about 0.24. A factor of three, and it reflects the reference, not the product. The
correction is not uniform across products or places, which is why a single scaling
factor cannot substitute for adjudication against a second reference.

**Some damage escapes everything.** About 11% of field-reported damage points, mostly in
inland hill communities, had no flag from any product within 20 m, despite lying inside
product analysed extents. These are collective misses in the areas where response
attention was already thinnest, and they are invisible to any evaluation that stays on
the coast. Taken together, the products still find nearly all field-reported damage:
within the core region, at least one of the six flagged within 20 m of 96% of field
points (97% of complete destruction, 87% of significant damage). The ecosystem's combined
recall is genuinely high; the inland gap is the shared blind spot within it.

![Field-reported damage points coloured by how many of the five extent-publishing
products flagged damage within 20 m (UNEP, which publishes no extent, is not counted
here). The coastal strip is well covered. The inland cluster was missed by
everyone.](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2_chatmap_found_by.png)

A final observation completes the picture. In the hard-hit coastal strip, the UH
product's flags have the best per-building precision of any single product. In
agricultural control areas where CEMS found essentially no damage, the same product
flagged up to 27.5% of buildings, in spatially clustered patterns that indicate
systematic model failure rather than noise. An evaluation confined to the damage-dense
strip would have certified a product that fails badly elsewhere.

**The pooled scorecard is one place's scorecard.** That cautionary tale generalizes,
and it bounds every headline number in this paper. CEMS activated five separate AOIs,
but 96% of its damage points sit in one of them: Caraballeda (1,468 points, against 26
in Morón, 14 in San Felipe, and 3 each in Caracas and Santa Cruz). Splitting the
scorecard by AOI (@fig-peraoi) shows two things. First, the pooled numbers *are*
Caraballeda's numbers — the per-AOI Caraballeda row reproduces the headline scorecard
almost exactly. Second, outside Caraballeda every product keeps flagging at scale —
IMPACT marks 9,445 buildings in the Caracas AOI, UH marks 32,145 (27.5% of the stock)
in Santa Cruz — while measured precision collapses to 0.00–0.02 everywhere. We state
plainly what those zeros can and cannot mean. They are floors against a reference that
recorded almost nothing in those AOIs, so two explanations are confounded: the products
hallucinating where damage is sparse (the same low-damage-zone mechanism as the UH
agricultural case and the Microsoft west strip), and CEMS under-recording damage in
AOIs it mapped thinly. The crowd cannot arbitrate here — the MapSwipe campaign
concentrated on the coastal strip, and at most 12% of these out-of-Caraballeda flags
fall on voted cells. Recall is measurable only in Morón (26 points), where the best
product finds 19% of it. What survives the ambiguity is the conditional: every
performance claim in this paper describes dense-damage coastal terrain, and in the four
low-damage AOIs the products' flags are almost entirely uncorroborated by any reference
we have.

Pooling all five AOIs gives the *as-delivered* scorecard — the product as a responder
received it, junk zones included. As-delivered precision: Microsoft 0.081, OSU 0.036,
IMPACT 0.032, UNEP 0.027, LIST 0.026, UH 0.009. Two things stand out. UH's number is
ten times worse than its best-case 0.093, because most of its flags sit in the
low-damage AOIs (32,145 in Santa Cruz alone). And Microsoft's number is *unchanged* —
not because its model behaves differently, but because it only published flags for the
coastal strip it had analysed carefully. Restraint in coverage is itself a product
property: shipping fewer, better-scoped zones protected Microsoft's as-delivered
precision, while shipping everywhere destroyed UH's. (The voting and fusion analyses of
@sec-dial operate in the core region and therefore sit on top of best-case numbers;
their relative orderings are unaffected, but their absolute levels inherit the
best-case flattery.)

Two mechanisms make the as-delivered numbers what they are, and both are worth stating
because they answer the obvious objection — *shouldn't precision be destroyed outside the
one dense zone?* The first is arithmetic. Because the four low-damage AOIs record almost no
damage, precision there is essentially zero, and the pooled figure is a flag-weighted
average — so a product's as-delivered precision falls by almost exactly the share of its
flags that land outside Caraballeda: Microsoft 0% of flags and 0% lost, OSU 17% and 16%,
IMPACT and LIST 52% and 52%, UNEP 68% and 68%, UH 90% and 90% (every product lands on the
diagonal *precision lost = share of flags in the dead zones*; plotted in @fig-deadzone,
in the Appendix). Precision is not *resisting* the false alarms; it collapses in direct
proportion to where each product chose to flag. The second mechanism means even this understates the problem: the
as-delivered frame can only score flags that fall inside a CEMS extent, and most products
flag far beyond one. Of each product's total flags, the share landing outside every CEMS
extent — where no reference can score them at all — is 4% for Microsoft but 43% for OSU,
71% for IMPACT, 76% for UNEP, and 79% for LIST. Since damage was concentrated on the coast,
the bulk of those unscoreable flags are almost certainly false positives. So every precision
figure in this paper, as-delivered included, is measured on each product's most favourable,
reference-covered subset; the true precision across a product's full output is very likely
lower, and unmeasurably so.

The as-delivered frame also re-runs this paper's harshest benchmark. We trained the
geography null model — coast distance, building density, and ShakeMap intensity, constructed
as described in @sec-dayzero — on each product's full delivered footprint under the same
spatially blocked validation, then cut its continuous risk score to *exactly* the number
of flags that product shipped. Compared this way, operating point against operating point
at each product's own delivered list size, **four of the six products are matched or
beaten by the geography null on both precision and recall**: IMPACT (product precision 0.032,
recall 0.55) against the null's 0.040 / 0.68; UH (0.009 / 0.37) against 0.022 / 0.92; LIST
(0.026 / 0.65) against 0.032 / 0.78; and UNEP (0.027 / 0.35) against 0.045 / 0.57 — at UH's own
list size the geography rule reaches 92% of the reference damage at more than twice UH's
precision. Only two products stay ahead of geography alone: Microsoft (0.081 / 0.55 against
0.053 / 0.36), which shipped only its carefully analysed strip, and OSU (0.036 / 0.85 against
0.032 / 0.77), which flagged so widely it bought recall the null could not match at that list
length. This result is unchanged by the matching radius: repeated at 20 m it is the same four
products, in the same direction (Appendix). One caveat cuts across all
of this: outside Caraballeda the reference is thin, and the penalty for flagging there
falls on the products, which did flag, not on the baseline, which did not. To whatever
extent CEMS under-recorded those areas, part of the gap would close. But a responder in
the first week had exactly the same information deficit, which is the point of the
as-delivered frame.

![Per-AOI scorecard, scorecard frame. Left: precision floor per product per CEMS AOI;
right: recall where the reference is thick enough to support it (suppressed below 20
CEMS points). Columns ordered by reference size; 96% of all CEMS damage points are in
the first column. Outside Caraballeda, measured precision is 0.00–0.02 despite flag
shares up to 27.5% — a floor against a nearly-empty reference, in which product
over-flagging and reference incompleteness cannot be separated with current data
("no overlap" = the product did not analyse that
AOI).](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2i_per_aoi_scorecard.png){#fig-peraoi}

## Results III — combining products: agreement as an operating point {#sec-dial}

### No single product can be tuned into a usable building list

Could a better single product fix per-building precision? Four independent experiments
in this event say no. The limit behaves like a property of the sensing method rather
than of any particular product. We refer to it as the modality ceiling: a precision level
that single-method tuning does not rise above. (Note that this is the opposite kind of
bound from the reference-driven lower bounds of @sec-crossexam: those mean the truth is
higher than measured; the ceiling means single-product performance stops improving.)

1. **Same-sensor agreement barely helps.** Requiring both Sentinel-1 coherence products
   (IMPACT and OSU) to agree raises precision only to 0.088, barely above the single
   products. Products that share sensor physics share false positives, so voting cannot
   remove them.
2. **A tunable rebuild saturates at the same level.** We built our own Sentinel-1
   amplitude-change product (per-pixel z-scores against a 30-scene pre-event baseline)
   and swept its threshold fully. Its best F1 (the harmonic mean of precision and
   recall — a single number that is only high when both are) ties the best shipped
   product, and no point on its curve approaches the multi-product rules. Its false alarms concentrated in
   farmland (8.0% of buildings flagged in an agricultural control area where CEMS found
   almost nothing), which confirms the advantage of radar coherence over amplitude for
   rural false alarms.
3. **Product confidence scores add nothing.** Sweeping Microsoft's continuous
   damage-fraction score (within its own analysed region, where its baseline numbers run
   higher than in the core region) trades recall 0.66→0.10 for precision 0.10→0.19. The
   shipped binary flag already sits near the best F1 on that curve. There is no hidden headroom
   in the confidence field.
4. **Agreement within one product plateaus too.** Microsoft flags corroborated by a
   second satellite scene are 2.5 times more precise than single-scene flags (0.245
   versus 0.097). That is a real gain and worth publishing. But it remains well below the
   strongest two-product rule (0.372), and in the low-damage zone where two scenes overlap, even flags
   confirmed by both scenes were rejected by 72% of crowd reviews. Agreement inside one
   model inherits that model's calibration failures.

### Agreement between independent methods is different

Voting across products works when their errors are independent — when two products
rarely make the same mistake in the same place. Requiring their agreement then removes
false positives faster than it removes real detections. The clearest example: pairing
Microsoft with UH, the product whose full-region precision is the worst we measured
(0.009, driven by the agricultural false alarms described above), produces the strongest
two-product rule in the study (precision at least 0.372, crowd-adjusted 0.64). Both are
optical products — and they even overlap in imagery source, since UH's authors confirm it
ran exclusively on Vantor imagery, the vendor behind several of Microsoft's scenes
including its failing one. What they do not share is the model, and that is where the
independence lives: their failure zones sit at opposite ends of the study area
(Microsoft's on the western coast, UH's in inland agriculture). A product with
serious failure zones is still a valuable voter wherever its errors are independent of
its partner's. The pair that shares its entire method — the two Sentinel-1 coherence
products — is by contrast the weakest of all fifteen pairings. We present this as a
mechanism, not a recipe: which pairing wins is probably event-dependent. The durable
claims are that error independence is the active ingredient, that sharing a sensing
method is the one reliable way to forfeit it, and that the usual day-one proxy —
modality diversity — did not predict the ranking here: the best pair shared a modality,
and the worst shared a method.

Scored against all three references at once, the number of agreeing products behaves as
a well-ordered operating point. Every step from 1-of-6 to 6-of-6 raises precision (both
the CEMS lower bound and the crowd-adjusted value) and lowers coverage:

| rule | flags | CEMS precision floor | crowd-adjusted precision | damage coverage (CEMS, 30 m) | visits per verified find (30 m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1-of-6 (union) | 37,644 | 0.03 | 0.21 | 0.97 | 26.5 |
| 3-of-6 | 9,409 | 0.10 | 0.28 | 0.86 | 7.5 |
| 4-of-6 | 3,347 | 0.19 | 0.38 | 0.67 | 3.4 |
| 6-of-6 | 214 | 0.64 | 0.93 | 0.18 | 0.8 |

: The voting rules, priced. "Crowd-adjusted precision" adds back the CEMS-unmatched flags
that MapSwipe volunteers judged damaged. "Damage coverage" is the share of CEMS damage
points with a flagged building within 30 m. "Visits per verified find" is the number of
flagged locations a responder must visit, per CEMS-verified damage point reached, at the
same 30 m scale. {#tbl-dial}

Two things should be read honestly from @tbl-dial. First, the false-positive cost is real
and dominates at low agreement: every single product wastes 80–86% of field visits even
at the generous 30 m scale (a wasted visit meaning a flagged stop with no CEMS damage
within 30 m), and the union wastes 89%. There are simply many more flags than damaged
buildings, and only requiring agreement pays that cost down. Second, the unanimous rule
is an anchor, not a practical operating point. It reaches near-certainty (crowd-adjusted
precision 0.93) but covers only 18% of the damage. Its value is what it reveals: 81% of
unanimous flags that CEMS did not record were judged damaged by the crowd, which makes
full agreement the sharpest available detector of the reference's own gaps, and a
ready-made field-validation queue for the reference provider.

![The six-member voting frontier, scorecard frame. Every marker is one flag list: grey
dots are the six products as shipped, hollow circles are two-product agreement rules
(the strongest, Microsoft ∧ UH, labeled), and the numbered blue squares are the k-of-6
voting rules from @tbl-dial. Each vertical whisker is that rule's precision *interval*:
the marker sits at the CEMS-measured floor, the whisker top at the crowd-adjusted value.
Single products cluster in the low-precision band at the bottom; each added vote of
required agreement trades recall for precision along the blue line. Whiskers adjust
precision only: adjudication re-judges flags and cannot add unrecorded damage to
recall's denominator, so in-frame recall is fixed — recall's own, downward uncertainty
is the grade-gradient result of
@sec-crossexam.](artefacts/RQ5-ensemble/figs/rq5b_frontier_r10.png)

### Weighted fusion, and the geography-only baseline

Flat voting weights every product equally. As a final step we fitted a logistic
regression that predicts per-building CEMS damage from the six flags, the products' own
confidence fields, and three context variables (building density, coastline distance,
shaking intensity). Validation is spatially blocked: the model is trained and tested on
disjoint ~5 km² zones, because neighbouring buildings share both features and labels and
a random split would leak that structure.

Because the models in this section output continuous scores rather than fixed flag lists,
they are compared on **average precision (AP)** — a metric that must not be confused with
precision itself. Precision and recall describe *one* flag list: the share of its flags
that are right, and the share of true damage it catches. AP describes a *score*: sweep
the score through every possible threshold, record the precision achieved at each level
of recall, and average — one number summarising the entire precision–recall curve. A high
AP means the score ranks damaged buildings ahead of intact ones well at every list size,
not that any particular list is precise. On this metric the weighted model reaches AP
0.284, against 0.194 for flat voting (the vote count 0–6 treated as a score), and a random
forest does no better than the logistic model — the useful signal is additive, and an
interpretable weighted vote captures essentially all of it.

That 46% AP advantage over flat voting should not be read as the practical margin, and the
reason is again a property of the metric rather than of the predictors. The vote count is an
*ordinal* score with seven levels, so it can be cut in only six places; its precision–recall
"curve" is six points, and integrating across them penalises the coarseness of the grid as
much as any deficit in ranking. Judged instead at the single operating point each would
actually be deployed at — the threshold maximising F1 — the gap narrows from 46% to **18%**
(voting 0.290 against fusion 0.343; @fig-bestf1).

That 18% is the price of the single most consequential distinction in this paper, and it is
worth paying deliberately. **The weighted fusion cannot be run during a response.** Its weights
are estimated from this event's reference labels — the very damage map a responder is waiting
for — so it is a retrospective instrument, subject to exactly the objection that disqualifies
the geography null as an operational tool (@sec-dayzero). Flat voting carries no such debt.
It requires no weights, no training data, and no reference: count how many products flag a
building. It is computable the hour the second product lands, by anyone, with a spreadsheet.

Set against that, the arithmetic is favourable. Voting reaches F1 0.290 where the best single
product manages 0.148 — **roughly twice the accuracy of any product taken alone** — and gives
up 18% against a fitted model that nobody could have fitted in time. On the evidence here,
counting agreement is the only method that is simultaneously effective and available on day
one, and that combination, rather than the fusion result, is what we would put in front of an
operational team.

Three qualifications keep the recommendation honest. First, "flat" conceals an assumption:
weighting every product equally means trusting them equally, and UH — whose as-delivered
precision was 0.009 — casts a full vote. That it *helped* rather than hurt is a real finding,
but one we could only establish with a reference in hand. Second, and following from the
pairwise results above, the transferable rule is not "count votes" but **"count agreement
between independent methods"**: the pair sharing its entire method was the weakest of all
fifteen, and a slate of five products sharing one method would inherit their common bias no
matter how many of them agreed. What products share — sensor, platform, model — is knowable
without labels, so this sharpens the rule rather than weakening it; this event also showed
the converse, in that the two optical products with nothing else in common formed the
strongest pair. Third, the choice of *k* remains, and while it can be made without labels — flag counts
are observable, so "we can visit three thousand buildings, therefore k = 4" is a legitimate
day-one decision — the precision that choice buys is not knowable at the time. A responder
picking k is choosing a workload, not a guaranteed hit rate.

The ablation is the result worth remembering. With the product inputs removed, the
geography null model (coast distance, building density, ShakeMap intensity — inputs available
within hours of the shaking, though the fit itself is retrospective; @sec-dayzero) reaches
AP 0.060. Since a single product is one binary flag list, not a score, it has no meaningful AP
of its own to set beside that number; the honest comparison is made point-against-curve. Every
threshold on the null score is a flag list, so its precision–recall curve is a whole family of
no-satellite predictors (@fig-geobaseline), and each product is one point in that plane.

Reading those points against the curve at **matched list sizes** — cutting the null at whatever
threshold produces exactly as many flags as that product shipped, so the two lists are the same
length and directly comparable — the products' advantage is slight and not universal. Three
products clear the null: UH (precision 0.093 against 0.065 at 5,362 flags), UNEP (0.086 against
0.068) and Microsoft (0.081 against 0.073). The other **three fall below it on precision and
recall alike**: IMPACT (0.069 against 0.071), LIST (0.057 against 0.062) and OSU (0.045 against
0.047). Even in the region where every product scores best, geography is not a floor the
products clear comfortably — half of them do not clear it at all, and the gap to fusion dwarfs
every one of these margins.

A second like-for-like comparison sharpens the same point and is easier to read, because it
puts every predictor on one number at one operating point. A provider ships exactly one flag
list, so a product's F1 is simply that list's F1. Our three continuous scores can be cut
anywhere, so we report each at its best single cut. That raises an obvious objection — the
products' thresholds were fixed by their providers without ever seeing the reference, while
ours are chosen knowing the labels — so we tested how much that asymmetry is worth. Selecting
the null model's threshold strictly out-of-sample, on an inner validation split held out from
the training blocks and then applied blind to the test fold, gives F1 0.129 against 0.128 for
the hindsight-chosen cut — a difference of 0.001. Hindsight buys nothing here, and at this
sample size a single scalar cut is estimated closely from training data alone.

The result is that geography sits *inside* the product range rather than beneath it. The null
reaches **F1 0.128** against 0.148 for the strongest product, UH — a shortfall of about 14% —
while matching or beating three of the six: IMPACT 0.123, LIST 0.104 and OSU 0.085. The two
remaining products, Microsoft (0.142) and UNEP (0.139), sit between (@fig-bestf1). No product
separates itself from a geography-only model by a margin that would survive a change of
reference or a redrawn study area. Two clarifications keep this from being read for more, or
less, than it is worth.

The first concerns average precision, which should not be used to make this comparison at all
even though it is the obvious summary to reach for. A product's AP looks superficially
comparable to the null's, but the two are different quantities: the null's is a genuine
integral over a full precision–recall curve, while a binary flag list's evaluates to
$P\cdot R + (1-R)\pi$ as described in @sec-dayzero, a value compressed toward prevalence that
lands near 0.08 for almost any product regardless of quality. Comparisons on that metric are
coincidences of value, not statements about performance, which is why the operating-point
comparison above is the one we rely on.

The second is what geography's parity does and does not imply. It does not mean the products
are uninformative: combining them reaches F1 0.290 by flat voting and 0.343 by weighted
fusion, well over twice the best single product and well beyond anything geography alone attains, so
there is real and complementary information in the set. What it means is that **no individual
product, in the region where all of them score best, separates itself clearly from a
hindsight model built on coastline distance, building density and shaking**. The value in
these products is in their disagreements with each other, not in any one of them taken alone.
And the two frames read consistently: where the products were carefully analysed they roughly
tie the geography null; across everything they actually shipped, most fall below it.

![Like-for-like at one operating point each. Grey bars: the six products at the single flag
list each provider shipped — the threshold was their choice, so this is simply that list's F1.
Coloured bars: our scores at their best single cut. The **geography null (logistic, 0.128)** is
the primary null and lands inside the product range, above IMPACT, LIST and OSU and below

with the weaker learner, shown for robustness and more favourable to the products

Appendix.](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8_best_f1_r10.png){#fig-bestf1}

Combination, flat or weighted, is what changes the picture — not any single product, and not
geography alone.

![The geography null model, in three views. **Top — the map**: colour is the damage risk
predicted by a model with no satellite input, only coast distance, building density, and
