## Results IV — diagnosing a product failure from its own metadata {#sec-casestudy}

Results I left the Microsoft west-strip anomaly unexplained. It can now be resolved
completely, and the resolution is the paper's best argument for metadata transparency.

The crowd settles what the cluster is. In the western strip, volunteers judged 71% of
Microsoft-flagged locations "no damage", against a roughly even split in the damage-dense
east. Independent people looking at post-event imagery saw nothing at most of the places
the cluster flags. The cluster is real over-detection, not a gap in the reference.

The product's own metadata explains where it came from. Every building in the strip has
`num_observations = 1`: the zone was covered by exactly one satellite scene. The platform
behind the product (HASTE; Robinson, Ortiz et al. 2026) trains a fresh model for each
scene and uses agreement between overlapping scenes as its only internal check. The west
never got that check. Cloud is ruled out as an alternative explanation: the west is the
most cloud-free zone in the product, and the visibility check in Methods moved nothing.
Splitting the product at the scene boundary shows what the headline number was hiding.
The single-scene west flags 28.7% of its buildings, with precision 0.05 and F1 0.10. The
multi-scene east flags 7.6%, with precision 0.21 and F1 0.30, the best single-product
zone we measured anywhere in this study. The same product contains both.

A head-to-head test of the two overlapping scenes pins down the mechanism. Scored
independently on the ~24,700 buildings both scenes covered, the "better" scene's
advantage turns out to be restraint, not accuracy: it flags 4.9% of buildings against the
other's 27.8%, but its flags are crowd-confirmed at a lower rate (7% versus 14%).
Microsoft's merge rule, which resolved conflicts in favour of that scene, was
directionally right (68% of the overruled flags were crowd-rejected) but silently
discarded roughly 845 flags on buildings the crowd judged damaged. And buildings flagged
by both scenes were still 72% crowd-rejected in this low-damage zone. The failure unit is
the calibration of each per-scene model, not the satellite, the provider, or the product
as a whole.

A cross-product control seals that attribution. UH's authors confirm their analysis ran
exclusively on Vantor imagery — the same commercial source as the failing scene — and over
the same strip UH shows the opposite pattern: it flags 3.4% of buildings in the west at
precision 0.138 (its best zone anywhere), against Microsoft's 32.4% at 0.033. Same imagery
vendor, different model, no cluster; the failure travelled with the per-scene calibration,
not the pixels. (UH's acquisition dates are unconfirmed, so this is vendor-level rather
than scene-level evidence.)

Three things about this case study generalize. First, a single product-level metric
averaged over a 4× internal quality split, and the split was only detectable because
per-building provenance was published. Second, the provider's own validation missed the
failure: the failing scene was exactly the one absent from their labeled validation set,
and the platform's previous external evaluation (Turkey) showed the opposite bias,
conservative under-flagging. Per-scene behaviour in a new event was not predictable from
the track record. Third, the diagnosis was available during the response: the crowd
campaign that rejected 71% of the strip's flags finished within days of the flags being
published, but no channel existed to carry that signal to the provider. For the five
products that publish no per-building provenance, we can show that they fail but never
why.

### A version postscript: what a product revision changes

One provider revised its product after the study window: OSU delivered a v1 on 22 July
(confidence tiers, ~8% expanded coverage, 69,431 flags versus v0's 58,870). The paper
scores v0 throughout, because v0 is what responders had during the response; the
operational dashboard has moved to v1. Since both versions key to the same building
base, they can be scored identically on the common extent against the same 1,488 CEMS
points (this comparison spans OSU's full extent, so its precision runs lower than the
core-region scorecard figure). The result: precision 0.036 (v0) versus 0.034 (v1),
recall 0.68 versus 0.64 — no measurable accuracy change — while **more than half the flag list turned over** (v1
dropped 30,565 of v0's 57,066 flags and added 42,723 new ones). A revision that
relabels half the buildings without moving precision or recall is itself evidence for
this paper's central reading: at the individual-building level these products are
noise-dominated, and version-to-version stability deserves a place beside accuracy in
how such products are judged. The area-level signal, by contrast, is robust to exactly
this kind of churn.

## Results V — timeliness: when the products arrived {#sec-timeline}

The operational question a scorecard cannot answer alone is *when*: a modestly accurate map
on day two can matter more than a better one on day eight. We reconstruct each product's
availability from the earthquake using the earliest date we can defend — the timestamp at
which each product was integrated into our own pipeline — which is a conservative *upper
bound* on when it was actually available (true provider-release dates are earlier and are
still being confirmed).

![Product availability, measured from the M7.5 mainshock. Circles mark a release or version;
a filled star marks the final product actually evaluated (Microsoft's merged union; IMPACT
v2). Positions are our-integration dates — an upper bound on availability — so true release
is earlier. Red markers are dates still to confirm.](timeline/timeline_products.png){#fig-timeline}

Three points stand (@fig-timeline). First, the entire ecosystem arrived inside about eight
days — the field went from nothing to a dozen independent products in a single week.
Second, several products were not single artefacts but sequences: Microsoft delivered
scene-by-scene across five areas before merging them into the union we evaluate, and both
IMPACT (raster v1 → vector v2) and OSU (v0 → a later v1) shipped successive versions — so
"the product" has a delivery history, and the version a responder acted on depended on when
they looked. Third, and honestly, we stop at *availability*: the decision-relevant analysis
— accuracy interacted with arrival date, so that a fast-but-rough product can be scored
against a slow-but-better one — requires confirmed provider-release dates we do not yet
hold, and is deferred. What the timeline already shows is that timeliness varied by days
across products, enough to matter operationally.

## Discussion

Two negative results are worth recording because they close tempting shortcuts. First,
reference-free reliability prediction failed. Spatial signatures of the flags themselves
(their rate, their clustering, even cross-product agreement) do not predict measured
reliability across areas; all correlations were non-significant over fifteen product-area
pairs. The reasons are structural. Pathological flags cluster the same way real damage
clusters, so clustering statistics cannot separate a severity gradient from a land-cover
artifact without reference data. And error decorrelation, which is decisive at building
level, does not aggregate: products' failure zones overlap regionally even when their
building-level errors are independent. Assessing reliability beyond a reference's
coverage therefore requires field or crowd data, or models trained across multiple
events. Second, and more positive: within reference coverage, local spatial statistics do
localize known failures. Local indicators of spatial association turn each product's
region into a reliability surface, with 78–86% of territory showing locally random error
(the benign regime) and the failures concentrated in identifiable pockets. That suggests
reliability-aware fusion, weighting votes by local error structure, as a natural next
step; we develop it in the register but do not rely on it here.

The strongest way to harden every claim in this paper is replication, and a specific
candidate exists: the 2025 Myanmar earthquake has a comparable multi-product,
crowd-validated landscape. The method transfers as-is. Whether the modality ceiling, the
monotone ordering of the voting rules, and the grade gradient hold there is exactly what
one event cannot establish.

## Recommendations

The results above imply changes in practice for three audiences. We collect them here,
once, rather than threading them through the analysis.

::: {.callout-tip title="For responders"}
**Do not spend time choosing a product; spend it counting agreement between products.** On
this event no single product was meaningfully better than a model of coastline distance and
building density, but the number of products agreeing on a building roughly doubled the
accuracy of any of them alone — and unlike a fitted model, counting requires no weights, no
training data and no reference, so it can be done the hour the second product arrives. Weight
the count toward *independent methods*: products that share a sensing method fail together
and their agreement carried the least information in our tests, while products with nothing
in common but the event cover for each other's failure zones. Then set the threshold from your own capacity — @tbl-dial gives
the flag counts and visit costs at each level — remembering that you are choosing a workload,
not a guaranteed hit rate. Used at sector scale, any major product ranks where to go first: trust that ranking, not the
building counts — while noting that coarse geography ranks about as well, so the ranking is
useful without being evidence that the product saw anything the map did not. Nothing in the current ecosystem sees lighter
damage reliably, so plan shelter assessments accordingly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="For providers"}
Publish an analysed extent; without one, a product cannot be evaluated or safely used.
Publish per-building acquisition metadata (scene count and dates); those fields are what
allowed this paper to trace a failure to its cause. Surface corroboration to users as a
confidence tier rather than leaving it in an archive column. Validate where the product
is deployed, not where validation data happens to exist; the failing scene here was the
unvalidated one. Check new products against a geography-only baseline, which every single
product in this event merely tied. And accept feedback during the activation: a crowd
campaign rejected 71% of one zone's flags within days, and no channel existed to carry
that signal back while reprocessing could still help.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="For evaluators and coordinators"}
A single expert reference understates precision most where damage is lighter. Publish
measured precision as a lower bound, or better, adjudicate the disputed flags against a
second reference and publish the interval. Note that unanimous product agreement without
expert corroboration turned out to be mostly real damage, so consensus doubles as a
detector of reference gaps and a field-validation queue. Finally, coverage is an
ecosystem property: the inland communities missed by every product were inside analysed
extents, and nobody knew that nobody was seeing them. A shared, live picture of who is
looking where costs providers nothing and closes the one gap here that no amount of
fusion can.
:::

## Limitations

This is one event in one coastal, dense-urban geography, and the core comparison region
is only ~61 km². More restrictive still, 96% of the CEMS reference sits in a single AOI
(Caraballeda), so every pooled number is effectively that AOI's number; in the four
low-damage AOIs, measured precision (0.00–0.02) cannot distinguish product
over-flagging from reference incompleteness (@fig-peraoi). The specific rule orderings
and magnitudes are hypotheses elsewhere. The
independence-versus-shared-method contrast rests on a single same-method pair (the two
coherence products); UH's exclusively-Vantor optical basis is author-confirmed, while
LIST's SAR basis remains provider-stated rather than documented. The crowd
reference was seeded from two AI products' flags, so it scrutinizes products unevenly
(100% of one product's contested zone had crowd votes, versus 59% for another) and cannot
see any product's misses. Crowd volunteers are not damage-assessment experts. Their
imagery, identified from the campaign's tile configurations, was fresh post-event VHR
(Vantor WorldView-3 via OpenAerialMap, acquired one to six days after the quake). The
contested western strip's scene is confirmed as 27 June from embedded metadata, two days
after the AI's problem scene, so damage persistence makes the crowd's rejections there
conservative; acquisition dates for some other areas rest on upload bounds rather than
image tags. Field reports are undated, positives-only, and skewed toward destruction
(79% complete), and their collection area is undefined, so the inland-gap estimate is a
lower bound. The voting analysis inherits the shared footprint base, where co-flagging
can fail for alignment reasons as well as genuine disagreement, so unanimous-rule recall
is understated. The learned fusion weights are calibrated within this event, and the same
applies to the geography null model, in a way that matters for how its result is read: the
baseline is fitted to this event's reference labels, so although it is scored strictly
out-of-fold on the same buildings as the products, it enjoys an event-specific calibration
the products never had and no responder possessed on the actual day zero. It is an upper
bound on geography-only skill, and the claim it supports is about information content — the
products add little beyond three context variables — rather than about what was operationally
in hand. A prior model fitted on *previous* earthquakes, which is what a responder would
really have, would score somewhere below this bound and remains untested here; building and
transferring one is the single clearest way to convert this null into an operational claim.
How much the null knows about the event itself also varies by layer, and the core-region
result is the weaker of the two: there ShakeMap intensity is effectively constant and
contributes nothing (importance 0.000), so the null reduces to static geography whose
discrimination comes entirely from hindsight fitting, whereas across the full delivered
footprints shaking carries 0.25–0.31 of the importance and the null is using genuinely
day-zero-available event information. OSU's
revised v1, delivered after the study window, is used by the operational dashboard but
enters this paper only in the dedicated comparison (@sec-casestudy); all other OSU
numbers are v0. Bootstrap
confidence intervals and population-weighted prioritisation are in progress and absent from
this draft. The timeliness axis is partly built: @sec-timeline reconstructs *availability*
(as an upper bound), but the decision-relevant interaction of accuracy with arrival date
awaits confirmed provider-release dates. Input imagery details and release dates for two
products (UH, LIST) await provider confirmation.

## Conclusion

Six damage products that disagree building by building agree, measurably and usefully, about
where this earthquake did its worst. But none of them stands out, and the comparison that
matters is not between products. In the region where all six score best, no single product
separates itself clearly from a model built on coastline distance, building density and shaking
alone; across their full delivered footprints, four of six place their flags no better than
that; and at the neighbourhood scale where they are genuinely usable, the same model ranks areas about
as well as they do — beating five of six across all mapped areas, though splitting three-three
within the damage zone itself. The value in this ecosystem is not in picking the right product,
because on this evidence there was no right product to pick.

It is in their disagreement. Because the products fail in different ways — and agreement is
most informative between products that share no method — the number that agree on a
building is a usable confidence measure, and counting that agreement roughly doubles the
accuracy of any product alone. That result carries an operational weight the rest of this paper
does not. A weighted fusion scores higher, but its weights are learned from the reference map a
responder is still waiting for; like the geography baseline, it is an instrument for
understanding an event afterwards, not for working through one. Counting agreement
needs no weights, no training data and no reference, costs about 18% against the fitted model,
and can be computed the hour the second product arrives. **It is the only method we tested that
is both effective and available on day one**, and it is the finding we would hand to a response
team.

What made any of this visible was not a better product but better references: three imperfect
datasets whose blind spots do not overlap, and which, turned on the expert reference itself,
showed that every published precision figure is a lower bound. The remaining practical changes
are collected in the Recommendations rather than repeated here. One finding stands apart from
all of them: as of this event, everything, products and references alike, sees destruction, not
damage.

## Appendix {.unnumbered}

### The 20 m label radius {.unnumbered}

All CEMS-based results in this paper use a 10 m matching radius (@tbl-allframes), and every
model is fitted and evaluated at that radius. The fusion analysis was originally built at
20 m out of concern for fit stability — 20 m labels 2,733 buildings damaged in the core region
against 1,350 at 10 m — and that frame is retained here as the sensitivity check. The same
analysis run end-to-end at 20 m gives:

| | evaluated at 10 m (reported) | evaluated at 20 m |
|---|---|---|
| best single product | 0.148 (UH) | 0.212 (MS, IMPACT) |
| geography null | 0.128 | 0.206 |
| null as a share of the best product | 86% | 97% |
| products the null matches or beats (best-F1) | 3 of 6 | 4 of 6 |
| flat k-of-6 voting | 0.290 | 0.342 |
| weighted fusion | 0.343 | 0.386 |
| fusion as a multiple of the best product | **2.3×** | 1.8× |

: F1 at each predictor's operating point under both label radii. {#tbl-radius}

Every conclusion in the paper holds under both. The wider radius raises all absolute values,
because a flag one building away from a recorded damage point starts to count as a hit. It
also flatters the geography null specifically, for a reason worth understanding: a wide radius
smears each reference point into a blob of neighbouring buildings, making the target
area-shaped, which is exactly the shape a smooth spatial predictor captures well. The tighter
10 m label concentrates the positives onto individual buildings, where per-building
discrimination is required — and there the case for *combining* products strengthens, from 1.8×
to 2.3× the best single product. Reporting at 10 m is therefore both the more consistent choice
and the more demanding one.

![Why as-delivered precision falls the way it does. Each product's as-delivered precision
(y) is plotted against the share of its flags that land outside Caraballeda (x), where the
reference records essentially no damage. Every product lies on the diagonal — precision
lost equals the share of flags in the dead zones — so the as-delivered precision is
governed almost entirely by *where* a product chose to flag, not by any resistance to false
alarms. Microsoft is spared only because it flagged nowhere else. This is the arithmetic
behind the first mechanism in
@sec-crossexam.](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2m_deadzone_dilution.png){#fig-deadzone}

### How the crowd adjustment works — and what happened when the crowd voted again {.unnumbered}

Every crowd-adjusted precision in this paper comes from one simple rule, and
@fig-crowdmech shows it acting on a real street in Catia La Mar. A flagged building with
an expert damage point within 10 m counts as a hit outright; the crowd plays no part in
that. Every other flag sits inside one of the ~50 m cells that MapSwipe volunteers voted
on, and the rule is: if most volunteers who saw that cell said *yes, damaged*, the flag is
counted as confirmed damage and improves the adjusted precision; if they said *no* or *not
sure*, it stays a false alarm. Flags in cells the volunteers never saw are assumed to
contain damage at the same rate as the flags the volunteers did see.

In August 2026 — after this paper's numbers were frozen — the campaign over this strip was
run a second time: 728 new volunteers re-judged exactly the same 3,482 cells, and each
cell now received about sixteen votes instead of six. Same buildings, different people, a
much harder look. Two caveats keep this from being a perfect replication. The answer
buttons changed: round 2 offered no "no damage" option, so a volunteer who saw nothing
wrong had to press "not sure" — which means round 1's headline finding for this strip
(71% of cells actively judged undamaged) simply cannot be re-measured. And the two rounds
showed volunteers different, though similarly dated, satellite images.

What can be compared across the rounds is how much damage the crowd *confirmed*, and that
held up. Of Microsoft's 7,661 flags in this strip with no expert match, the first crowd
confirmed 13.2%; the second, deeper-looking crowd confirmed 11.5%. Two independent juries
agree that roughly one flag in eight has crowd-visible damage under it. If anything, the
harder look confirmed slightly *less*, so the crowd-adjusted values in this paper should
be read as sitting a little high — consistent with their stated role as upper estimates.

What did not hold up is *which* cells were confirmed: only about a quarter of the cells
the first crowd confirmed were confirmed again by the second (the purple outlines in
@fig-crowdmech). That sounds alarming until one asks how much two small juries should
agree even if volunteers were perfectly consistent — and the answer is, not much. Six
votes on a borderline cell is close to a coin toss, and once that known voting noise is
accounted for, the two rounds' underlying judgements agree well (correlation 0.63, versus
0.29 before the correction). Most of the apparent chaos is small vote counts, not fickle
volunteers. The practical lesson is the one this paper already follows: a single cell's
verdict is too noisy to lean on, but sums over thousands of cells are steady — which is
why crowd verdicts appear here only inside aggregate numbers, never as building-level
ground truth.

Finally, the cost in numbers. Recomputing each product's crowd-adjusted precision with the
second round's verdicts in place of the first moves it by at most 0.03 in either
direction: Microsoft's falls from 0.237 to 0.223, UNEP's from 0.074 to 0.043 (nearly all
of its crowd-reviewed flags sit in this one strip), and IMPACT's and UH's tick slightly
upward. No product overtakes another.

![How the MapSwipe crowd enters the precision calculation, and what an independent re-vote
changed. Both panels show the same Catia La Mar neighbourhood; hexagons are the ~50 m crowd
task cells, tinted by majority verdict. **A** — round 1: a flag matched by an expert point
within 10 m is a true positive (green); an unmatched flag in a cell the crowd judged
damaged is counted as confirmed and improves the adjusted precision (blue); in a cell
judged undamaged or uncertain it remains a false alarm (orange). **B** — round 2 re-voted
the identical cells at ~16 votes each, with no "no damage" answer available (its "not
sure" absorbs it): purple outlines mark cells whose verdict changed sides. Individual
cells flip; the total the adjustment depends on barely moves (13.2% → 11.5% of the
strip's unmatched Microsoft flags confirmed).](artefacts/RQ7-mapswipe-validation/figs/rq7_crowd_adjustment_explainer.png){#fig-crowdmech}

## Reproducibility note {.unnumbered}

All analyses run from immutable data snapshots, frozen on 2026-07-15 and stored as
Parquet, GeoParquet, CSV, and GeoJSON files in the project's Azure blob storage.
Per-question scripts, running notes, and the full findings register, including every
negative and superseded result, accompany this draft in the project repository.
